item.title: Spectrum, Containers, Durable Objects, Workers - Inbound TCP and gRPC for Workers and Containers now in public beta
item.description:
Inbound TCP connections to Workers and bidirectional gRPC in Containers are now in public beta.

Worker-origin Spectrum applications are available on Pro and Business zones, and on Enterprise zones with Spectrum Enterprise enabled. Without Spectrum Enterprise, Pro and Business zones support one Worker-origin application per zone, on one TCP port.

    Spectrum <--> Worker["Worker connect()<br/>Handle or forward bytes"]
    Worker <--> DO["Durable Object<br/>connect()"]
    DO <--> Container["Container<br/>gRPC or other TCP server"]

Forward a Worker socket to a Durable Object

Spectrum sends public TCP connections to your Worker's connect() handler. The Worker opens a socket to the GrpcContainer Durable Object and pipes bytes in both directions:

Forward the Durable Object socket to its Container

The Durable Object receives the connection in its own connect() handler. Once its Container is running, getTcpPort(50051).connect() opens a socket to the gRPC server inside it:

allowHalfOpen: true preserves TCP half-closes. The Worker and Durable Object forward encrypted bytes; the Container terminates TLS and handles HTTP/2 and gRPC.

Run bidirectional gRPC in the Container

Run an existing gRPC server in any language, including services for real-time voice applications. This Node.js snippet shows the streaming handler and service registration. It sends a greeting, echoes incoming messages, and sends a final response when the client finishes:

item.title: Workers, Pages - Workers and Pages now keep versions for 30 days
item.description:
Cloudflare now keeps versions of your Workers and deployments of your Pages projects for 30 days. After 30 days, they are deleted, except your 100 most recent and what is currently deployed.

What is not affected:

  • Running applications: Deployed Worker versions and your current Pages production deployment are always kept
  • Rollbacks: You can still roll back to any of your 100 most recent Worker versions, and to any Pages production deployment that has not been deleted
  • Worker Previews: Worker Preview URLs always serve the latest deployment of that Preview. Use Worker Previews for branches and pull requests instead of Version URLs, which run with your production bindings

What you will notice:

  • Deleted versions and deployments no longer appear in the dashboard or API
  • The URL associated with each deleted Worker version, known as its Version URL (including any --preview-alias), stops working, as does the preview URL of each deleted Pages deployment

For more information, refer to Workers version retention, Pages deployment limits, and Compare workflows.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Cloudflare CLI (cf) 1.0 release candidate
item.description:
Cloudflare CLI (cf) 1.0.0-rc.1 is a release candidate for cf 1.0. cf has been in beta since late September. This is the release we recommend you try on your own projects, and we want your feedback before 1.0.

To install or update to the latest release:

npm install --global cf@latest
yarn global add cf@latest
pnpm add --global cf@latest
bun add --global cf@latest

What is stable

We expect the following features to remain stable to cf 1.0:

  • The cloudflare.config.ts configuration format.
  • The Build Output format that cf build writes and cf deploy reads.
  • The commands that create, develop, build, and deploy projects, including cf init, cf dev, cf build, cf deploy, cf previews deploy, and cf workers versions create.
  • The large majority of commands generated from the Cloudflare API and used in the beta.

A small number of less commonly used API commands may still change before 1.0. cf generates these commands from the Cloudflare API schema, so their call path may still change before 1.0.

Upgrade from a beta

This release moves Build Output to version 1, in .cloudflare/output/v1/. cf deploy will automatically create a new build on first run in this location.

The release candidate also moves to caret (^) version ranges for its dependencies, requiring:

  • @cloudflare/vite-plugin 2.0.0-rc.0 or later, for projects that build with Vite.
  • Wrangler 4.163.0 or later, for legacy projects that build with Wrangler.

1.0.0-rc.1 renames a few generated API commands without aliases. For example, cf workers secrets bulk is now cf workers secrets bulk-edit. For the full list, refer to the release notes ↗︎.

If you last updated early in the beta, these earlier changes may also affect you:

  • Prompts, progress, and status messages are written to stderr. Stdout holds only command output, so scripts that read messages from stdout must read stderr instead.
  • Commands generated from camelCase or snake_case API names use kebab-case. For example, cf accounts billing getCredits is now cf accounts billing get-credits.
  • cf previews deploy takes the Preview name as --preview-name instead of a positional argument.
  • Commands run with --local store state in the project's .cloudflare/state directory.
  • cf no longer saves your account choice between runs. Set accountId in cloudflare.config.ts or CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID to skip the prompt.
  • Streaming tail consumers move to experimental.streamingTailConsumers in cloudflare.config.ts.
  • Destructive commands run without a terminal exit with an error unless you pass --force.
  • cf supports the latest versions of the Node.js LTS releases and the latest active release of Node.js.

Stream live logs

cf observability tail streams live logs and other observability events as newline-delimited JSON. Select a Worker with --worker, a zone and its subdomains with --zone, or every event in the account with --all. Narrow the results with --filters, as inline JSON or from a file:

Worker events require Workers Logs to be turned on for the Worker. For filter shapes and examples, run cf observability tail --help.

What changed during the beta

Deploy

  • Deploy a directory of static assets with cf deploy ./dist. cf skips the build step and creates an assets-only Worker.
  • cf deploy --no-provision fails when a binding has no resource ID, instead of creating a new resource.
  • cf deploy --force deploys when the Worker was last deployed through the API, or when its remote configuration conflicts with your local Build Output.
  • Redeploying no longer removes secrets that you added outside cloudflare.config.ts.
  • Stack traces from deployed Workers show project paths such as src/index.ts.
  • Python Workers with vendored packages deploy correctly.
  • cf deploy applies SSH settings for Containers managed by Durable Objects.
  • cf deploy --dry-run shows the project setup changes it would make, without making them.
  • Set CLOUDFLARE_DEPENDENCIES_INSTRUMENTATION=false to stop uploading package dependency metadata with each deployment.

Develop

  • cf init creates new Worker projects with Vite+, including checks, formatting, and tests that run in the Workers runtime.
  • cf dev and cf build run the Vite or Vite+ executable installed in your project, including dependencies hoisted in a workspace.
  • cf dev passes arguments such as --port and --host to your framework's development server.
  • cf dev --profile <name> passes the selected authentication profile to your development server.
  • cf dev, cf build, and cf deploy offer to run cf migrate when they find a Wrangler configuration file.
  • On Windows, Ctrl+C exits cleanly when your framework runs through npm, Wrangler and Vite start without spawn EFTYPE errors, and cf d1 migrations create rejects names that Windows cannot store.
  • cf init approves the build scripts that pnpm 11 and later block by default, so installation succeeds.

Sign in and accounts

  • Pass --temporary-account to create a short-lived account without signing in. cf prints a URL you can use to claim the account.
  • cf auth login summarizes the scopes you granted, and cf auth scopes lists them by product.
  • cf auth whoami, also available as cf whoami, prints a short summary in a terminal and full JSON for scripts and agents.
  • cf auth login now uses the system keyring where available.
  • Long-running commands, such as cf observability tail, refresh an expired OAuth login instead of failing.
  • cf auth whoami reports the status of scoped API tokens correctly.
  • Set CLOUDFLARE_API_HEADERS to send custom headers with API requests.

API commands

  • Every command accepts --dry-run to preview what it would do and it redacts sensitive fields in request previews.
  • cf checks --body input before it asks you to sign in or confirm, and rejects array bodies larger than the API allows instead of splitting them across several requests.
  • More request fields are available as flags, including JSON objects and maps, arrays of objects, and file uploads. For example, cf pages deployments create --worker-js @./_worker.js and cf ai to-markdown --files @first.html @second.pdf.
  • Error outputs have been improved with additional messages the API returns, such as the names of missing parameters.
  • cf workers commands accept --worker to select a Worker.
  • --zone finds zones by name in accounts with many zones.
  • cf tunnels quick-start --allowed-mail limits a temporary tunnel to the email addresses and domains you allow.

Scripts and agents

  • cf --version prints only the version number.
  • Shell completions and cf tools list every flag a command accepts.
  • cf cli search has reranked cf deploy and other key commands to improve their ranking for static site and Pages deployment searches.
  • cf docs search finds Cloudflare documentation from the terminal.

Send feedback

To report a bug or tell us what is missing, open an issue in the cf repository ↗︎. For every change in each release, refer to the Cloudflare CLI release notes ↗︎.

item.title: Artifacts, Workers - Artifacts now supports local development
item.description:
You can now develop and test Artifacts locally. Create repos, import Git repositories over HTTPS, issue repo tokens, and clone or push with Git on your machine before deploying to Cloudflare's global network. Local repos are separate from your deployed repos, so you can test changes without affecting production data.

Local repos also emit the same Artifacts events as production when a repo is created, imported, forked, or deleted, or when a repo token is created or revoked. This lets you test the Workflows that react to them before you deploy.

To use local repos when you run your Worker locally, add an Artifacts binding to your Wrangler configuration file:

Run npx wrangler dev, then use the binding the same way you would in production:

The returned remote points to your local dev session, so you can use it with a standard Git client to clone and push.

Local development requires the latest version of Wrangler and Git 2.32 or later on your PATH.

When you develop with npx wrangler dev, the Cloudflare Vite plugin, or the Workers Vitest integration, Artifacts bindings use the local simulator by default. To use your deployed repos instead, set remote = true on the binding.

To learn more, refer to Local development.

item.title: Billing, Workers, Durable Objects - Set spending limits for Workers and Durable Objects
item.description:
You can now set spending limits for Workers and Durable Objects to help control unexpected usage costs, or receive email alerts while your applications keep running. Support for more products is coming soon.

Use these controls alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.

Workers and Durable Objects limits apply across your account for the current subscription billing period. Each product has its own spending controls.

Set your limits and alerts

In the Cloudflare dashboard ↗︎, select your account and go to Billing > Spend limits. Choose a spending limit, notification email, and alert thresholds for Workers or Durable Objects.

For example, configure a $10 Workers spending limit with email alerts at $5 and $9. To receive alerts while your applications keep running, turn off Block usage.

See when a limit takes effect

The overview shows each product's recorded spend, alert thresholds, and pause status. Email alerts notify you without stopping usage. When a spending limit takes effect, Cloudflare blocks the product's supported operations.

To resume usage, raise the limit above current spend, turn it off, or remove it. Usage also resumes when the next billing period starts.

Usage reporting and blocking take time, so recorded spend can exceed a limit. Read about what counts toward a limit.

Choose alerts, limits, or both

For example, set a $50 spending limit for Workers and a $20 email alert for Durable Objects:

flowchart LR
    A["Durable Objects reaches $20"] --> B["Email alert sent"]
    B --> C["Usage continues"]
    D["Workers reaches $50"] --> E["Spending limit takes effect"]
    E --> F["New Worker invocations blocked"]

Set a spending limit with the cf CLI

Install the cf CLI and select your account, then run this command to set a $50 spending limit for Workers usage in the current billing period:

The amount is in US cents: 5000 means $50. To set a spending limit for Durable Objects, use --product-id durable_objects and update the name. Limits count usage already recorded in the current billing period.

You can also give this prompt to your coding agent. It will ask which product you want to manage and what spending limit to set, then use the CLI to configure it.

Use spending limits alongside budget alerts

The budget alerts introduced earlier this year notify you about account-wide usage costs without stopping usage. You can keep using them alongside the new product-specific spending limits and email alerts for Workers and Durable Objects.

To configure account-wide alerts, go to Billing > Billable Usage or follow the budget alerts guide.

Read the spending limits and alerts guide to learn how spending limits work and manage limits and alerts through the dashboard or cf CLI.

Previously, to serve assets from /blog/, you had to nest your files in a matching blog directory. Now, set assets.base_path in your Wrangler configuration file, or worker.assets.basePath in cloudflare.config.ts, and keep your files at the root of your asset directory.

item.title: Workers, Pages - Workers Builds and Pages now list GitHub repositories based on your GitHub account
item.description:
When you connect a GitHub repository to Workers Builds or Pages, the accounts and repositories you can pick from are now based on your own GitHub account, so the list reflects the repositories you work with on GitHub. Previously, the list was based on the Cloudflare Workers & Pages GitHub App installations linked to your Cloudflare account, so it could include repositories that you cannot access on GitHub.

The list now shows:

  • Your own GitHub account, if the app is installed on it.
  • GitHub organizations that have the app installed, where you can access at least one repository.
  • The repositories you can access in each of them.

GitHub accounts that belong to other users are no longer listed, even if they have given you access to one of their repositories.

What this means for you:

Authorizing the app and installing it are two separate steps on GitHub. For more details, refer to Install and authorize the app for Workers Builds and Pages.

  • If you have already authorized the app with your GitHub user: Nothing changes. You can check on the Authorized GitHub Apps page ↗︎ on GitHub.
  • If you have not: The next time you connect a repository, Cloudflare sends you to GitHub to authorize the app. You only need to do this once, even if someone else on your Cloudflare account already connected GitHub.
  • If the app is not installed on any GitHub account you can access: After you authorize, install the app on your own GitHub account or an organization, the same as before.
  • If an account or organization is missing from the list: Select Add GitHub account and install the app on it.

Projects that are already connected to a repository are not affected and keep building.

For more information, refer to Repository access for Workers Builds and Pages.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Set a concurrency limit for each Workflow
item.description:
You can now set a concurrency limit on an individual Workflow to cap how many of its instances run at the same time. Use it to protect a database or third-party API that slows down or rejects requests past a certain number of concurrent connections, or to distribute load more evenly across your Workflows so that one high-volume Workflow does not use all of your account's concurrency.

For example, to allow only 10 instances of a Workflow to run at a time, set concurrency.limit on its workflows binding and redeploy:

You can also set concurrency on a Workflow declared in exports, or with exports.workflow() in @cloudflare/config.

Instances above the limit are not rejected. They are queued and start automatically as running instances finish or move to the waiting state.

The limit must be a positive integer, and cannot be higher than your account's concurrency limit (100 on Workers Free, 50,000 on Workers Paid). Lowering the limit does not stop instances that are already running. Workflows without a concurrency limit can still use up to your account's full concurrency limit.

Caution

Set concurrency.limit in your configuration on every deploy. If you deploy without it, the Workflow's concurrency limit is removed.

Per-Workflow concurrency limits require Wrangler 4.127.0 or above.

For more information, refer to Concurrency limits.

item.title: Workers, Agents - Run the Codex agent loop on Cloudflare Workers
item.description:
Run the Codex agent loop in a Cloudflare Durable Object with this experimental Agents SDK example ↗︎. Conversations, files, and completed model and tool results persist across restarts, allowing the agent to recover after interruptions.

The example adapts Codex’s Rust turn-processing code ↗︎ to WebAssembly and uses Agents SDK capabilities for storage and recovery.

The harness combines Agents SDK capabilities for durable execution:

  • Tasks journals model calls and tool execution. Completed steps reuse their recorded results after a restart. Interrupted steps can run again.
  • Sessions stores conversation history and compacts the model context.
  • Streams stores ordered events for replay after reconnecting.
  • Workspace provides tools to read and write persistent files.

For example, use OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol through AI Gateway. Configure the model with createAI and install the capabilities on a Durable Object:

To use this model, configure the default gateway with Unified Billing or a stored OpenAI API key.

For setup, models, tools, and recovery behavior, refer to the Codex harness guide.

item.title: Durable Objects, Workers - Automatic retries for Durable Object calls
item.description:
The runtime now retries fetch() and RPC calls to a Durable Object when they fail with a retryable error before reaching it. This applies whether the caller is a Worker or another Durable Object. Short disruptions, such as brief network interruptions, no longer need a retry loop in your code.

By default, the runtime retries a call up to four times, and starts no retry more than 10 seconds after the initial call starts. It does not retry errors thrown by your Durable Object code, or errors with .overloaded set to true.

If the connection drops and the runtime cannot tell whether the Durable Object received the call, it still retries, but the Durable Object rejects the retry if the first attempt arrived. A method never runs twice because of a retry, unless you mark it with retryable() from cloudflare:durable-objects:

To change the limits for one stub, pass a retry option to get() or getByName(). maxRetries accepts 0 to 10 retries, and timeoutMs accepts 500 to 60,000 milliseconds:

If you already retry Durable Object calls in your own code, each of your attempts now includes the runtime's retries. Lower your own attempt count, or set maxRetries: 0 on stubs where your code handles retries.

To use retryable() and the retry option, update to Wrangler 4.158.0 or later.

For more information, refer to Automatic retries.

item.title: Workers - Count weighted requests with the Rate Limiting binding API in Workers
item.description:
Requests can require different amounts of work. A product lookup might be cheap, while a search runs an expensive database query. Use weighted requests to make expensive operations consume more of the same rate limit.

The Rate Limiting binding now accepts an optional delta in limit(). Pass delta to choose how many units a call consumes.

For example, assign one unit to a product lookup and 10 units to an expensive search. Both operations consume the same user's allowance. The following handler takes a verified user ID from your application's authentication flow:

The delta defaults to 1. To use delta in local development, use Wrangler 4.157.0 ↗︎ or later. For TypeScript support, use @cloudflare/workers-types version 5.20261106.1 or later.

For more details, refer to Weighted requests.

item.title: Workers - Workers will use the new module registry by default on November 17
item.description:
Starting November 17, 2026, JavaScript Workers with a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later will use the new module registry by default. You will no longer need the new_module_registry flag for these dates. Python Workers keep using the legacy registry.

The module registry finds and loads JavaScript modules in your Worker. We announced the new registry in September 2026 ↗︎. It improves compatibility with JavaScript standards and Node.js. In Workers using Node.js compatibility, you can use require() to load ES modules. The module and its dependencies must not use top-level await.

You can also use import.meta to get information about the current module and find the URL of another module without loading it:

When deployed with src/index.ts as the unbundled entrypoint, isEntrypoint is true. helperUrl is a URL within your Worker bundle. Resolving the URL does not check whether the module exists or load it over the network. Build tools may transform import.meta. To try this example directly, refer to unbundled deployments.

Existing Workers keep their current behavior until you change their compatibility date or flags. To try the new registry before November 17, keep your current date and add new_module_registry to your compatibility flags.

Before updating, check your dependencies for invalid import attributes and changes to require() behavior. The new registry rejects invalid import attributes. Calls to require() also fail if the module or any of its dependencies use top-level await. To keep the legacy registry with a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later, add legacy_module_registry.

For migration details, refer to the new module registry compatibility flag, bundling documentation, and Node.js compatibility documentation.

item.title: Workers - Request.signal will be enabled by default in Workers on November 17
item.description:
Starting November 17, 2026, Workers with a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later will receive client disconnection events through request.signal by default. Use these events to stop unnecessary work when a client leaves. You will no longer need the enable_request_signal compatibility flag for these dates.

We introduced this feature in May 2025. You can log cancellations, clean up resources, or cancel operations that accept an AbortSignal.

For example, this Worker logs a client disconnection and cancels an outgoing request:

Existing Workers keep their current behavior until you change their compatibility date or flags. To try this feature before November 17, keep your current date and add enable_request_signal to your compatibility flags.

With a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later, add disable_request_signal to opt out. This change does not enable request_signal_passthrough. Pass the signal explicitly, as the example does.

For more information, refer to the Request API and the Request.signal compatibility flag.

item.title: Durable Objects, Workers - Durable Objects now defer code updates by default
item.description:
Durable Objects can stay active across requests, allowing you to run long-running agents, maintain long-lived WebSocket connections and coordinate state across many clients. This is possible because each Durable Object is globally unique, and this means it must run only one version of your code at a time. Previously, when you deployed a change to your Durable Objects code, that change would be applied immediately, which could interrupt in-flight work and terminate open connections.

Durable Objects now defer code updates by default. When you deploy, an active Durable Object can keep running its current code for up to 5 minutes (300 seconds) while it waits to hibernate. This gives in-flight work time to finish. WebSocket connections that use the Hibernation API remain connected when an object adopts new code after hibernating.

For an active Durable Object, a code update follows this flow:

flowchart TD
    accTitle: Code updates for an active Durable Object
    accDescr: By default, an active object can keep running its current code until it hibernates or the delay ends. After hibernating, it starts on new code on the next request. If the delay ends first, or immediate mode is selected, it resets and adopts the new code. Deferral is best effort.
    A["You deploy new code"] -->|"Default: deferred"| B["The object can keep running<br/>its current code"]
    B --> C{"Hibernates before<br/>the delay ends?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Starts on the new code<br/>on the next request"]
    C -->|No| E["The object resets<br/>and adopts the new code"]
    A -.->|"Override: immediate"| E

To change the delay, add code_update_strategy to durable_objects in your Wrangler configuration:

max_delay is in seconds, from 0 to 86400 (24 hours), with millisecond precision. Omit it to use the default of 300 seconds.

To set the strategy for a single deployment, pass --durable-objects-code-update-mode with immediate or deferred <duration>. For example, apply an update right away during an incident, or when your deployment tooling calls a Durable Object right after deploying and needs the new code:

npx wrangler versions deploy <VERSION_ID>@100% --durable-objects-code-update-mode immediate
yarn wrangler versions deploy <VERSION_ID>@100% --durable-objects-code-update-mode immediate
pnpm wrangler versions deploy <VERSION_ID>@100% --durable-objects-code-update-mode immediate

A deferred code update is best effort and does not guarantee that every operation finishes. The object can still reset before max_delay is reached, for example during a Cloudflare runtime update.

For more information, including how this interacts with gradual deployments and the REST API, refer to Durable Objects code updates.

item.title: Workers, BYOIP, Bots - Workers subrequests now preserve context for BYOIP destinations
item.description:
Cloudflare now preserves Workers context when a subrequest targets a Cloudflare-proxied hostname using Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP). These requests are identified as Cloudflare-to-Cloudflare traffic instead of external Internet traffic.

Previously, some BYOIP subrequests could lose Workers context and original client signals. This could cause security rules to behave unexpectedly, Bot Management to evaluate an internal Cloudflare connection instead of the original client, or affected requests to return false 403 responses.

Workers subrequests to BYOIP destinations now preserve the CF-Worker header and cf.worker.upstream_zone field. This supports consistent security rule evaluation across same-zone and cross-zone subrequests.

Bot Management fields on the destination zone now represent the original end-user connection for affected BYOIP subrequests. Bot scores, verified bot status, and JA3/JA4 fingerprints no longer represent the internal connection between Cloudflare services.

Because Cloudflare-proxied BYOIP destinations now follow standard Workers subrequest handling, cross-zone requests set CF-Connecting-IP to the Workers client IP address 2a06:98c0:3600::103 for security reasons. This applies when a Worker in one Cloudflare zone sends a subrequest to a hostname in another Cloudflare zone. Same-zone subrequests continue to reflect the client IP through CF-Connecting-IP.

For more information, refer to Cloudflare BYOIP, Workers subrequests, and CF-Connecting-IP in Worker subrequests.

item.title: Workers - Workers Builds now retains builds and build logs for 90 days
item.description:
Workers Builds now retains each build and its build logs for 90 days after the build finishes. You can find them under View build history in your Worker's Deployments tab, or through the Workers Builds API.

After 90 days, a build and its logs are removed. The versions and deployments it created stay in your Worker's version history, so you can still roll back to them.

If you need a build's logs for longer, you can download them with the Get build logs API endpoint.

For more information, refer to the Workers Builds limits documentation.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Restrict Workflows to a jurisdiction
item.description:
You can now restrict a Workflow to a jurisdiction. Its instances only run and store data within that jurisdiction, which helps you comply with data localization regulations such as GDPR ↗︎ or FedRAMP ↗︎.

Set jurisdiction on a workflows binding, or on a Workflow declared in exports:

The supported jurisdictions are eu (the European Union), us (the United States), and fedramp (FedRAMP-Moderate data centers).

A Workflow's jurisdiction is set when the Workflow is created, and cannot be changed afterwards. If an existing Workflow has a different jurisdiction, wrangler deploy and wrangler versions upload stop before uploading your Worker.

Workflow jurisdictions require Wrangler 4.152.0 or above.

For more information, refer to Data location.

item.title: Agents, Workers - Cloudflare Computer now helps agents recover from interruptions and wait for approval
item.description:
@cloudflare/computer ↗︎ gives your agent a workspace to run code in. From v0.7.0, that code can resume after a deploy or crash, and pause on an external action, for example to approve a tool call.

Resume interrupted runs

Set onInterrupt: "replay" on WorkerJavaScriptBackend, or on a single run.

When recovery is triggered, the JavaScript runs again from the beginning, reusing recorded results for completed calls without printing previously recorded output again. If a call's result was not recorded before the interruption, recovery may repeat the call — even if its action already succeeded. For retry handling, including unsafeToRepeat() for operations that cannot safely repeat, refer to Calls that must not run twice.

Recovery starts on the next call to workspace.runtime. To recover without waiting for traffic, call workspace.runtime.recover() from a Durable Object alarm.

Wait for approvals

Expose your application functions through custom modules. A function can call ctx.interrupt() to pause the run until your application supplies an approval decision.

Require approval before posting a comment

For example, to provide a GitHub module that allows an agent to post a comment on an issue with approval, an implementation of postComment could look like this:

Call it from agent code

When the agent's code calls postComment(), the run pauses at ctx.interrupt() until your app responds. The agent's code calls it like any other function:

Respond to the approval request

The time spent waiting does not count toward its timeout. The wait also survives deploys. Fetch the pending calls with workspace.runtime.pending() and resolve them with respond():

The run continues once all pending calls are resolved.

For setup, current limitations, and how replay works, refer to Resume runs after a restart.

item.title: Workers - Workers tracing — new spanContext(), setStatus(), and updateName() APIs
item.description:
Custom spans in Workers now support three more methods from the OpenTelemetry span API.

  • span.spanContext() returns the span's traceId, spanId, and traceFlags. The IDs match the trace and span IDs in Workers Observability and in exported traces, so you can log them or return them to clients to correlate a request with its trace.
  • span.setStatus(status) sets the span status to "unset", "ok", or "error", with an optional message for errors. Span status is included in traces exported to OpenTelemetry destinations. The Workers Observability dashboard does not display it yet.
  • span.updateName(name) renames a span after it starts, such as once you know which route a request matched. You can also rename the invocation's root span returned by tracing.getActiveSpan().

For more details, refer to the custom spans documentation.

item.title: Workers, Pages - Workers Builds and Pages build images reject compromised eMudhra certificates
item.description:
The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities ↗︎ can be recovered, so anyone can forge a certificate for any hostname that chains to them. The Workers Builds and Pages build images now reject these certificates when your build clones your repository, installs dependencies, or makes HTTPS requests.

The updated images include patched CA certificates, Node.js 22.23.4 and 24.22.1, Bun 1.4.4, and pip 26.2.2. Build commands also run with environment variables that point older runtimes at the patched CA certificates.

What you need to do

Most projects need no changes. Update your project if:

  • You set BUN_VERSION below 1.4.4. Older Bun versions trust the compromised certificates.
  • You set your own SSL_CERT_FILE, PIP_CERT, or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, or set --use-bundled-ca in NODE_OPTIONS. Make sure your CA certificates do not trust the compromised intermediates.
  • Your build installs tools that ship their own CA certificates. Update them to a version that removes the compromised intermediates.

For details, refer to the build image documentation for Workers Builds and Pages.

item.title: Workers - Pin your npm version in Workers Builds with packageManager
item.description:
You can now choose the npm version that Workers Builds uses by setting the packageManager field in your package.json. Before the build installs dependencies, it installs the npm version you set, so a lockfile written by a newer npm version installs the same way in your build as it does locally.

The packageManager field also sets the version of Yarn, pnpm, and Bun. Use an exact version, such as npm@11.19.1, not a range. Workers Builds does not use the engines.npm field to choose an npm version.

For more information, refer to Package manager versions.

item.title: Agents, Workers - Think agents now use a @cloudflare/computer workspace
item.description:
Think and Agent Skills now use the workspace from @cloudflare/computer ↗︎ as well as the filesystem tools. A JavaScript execution environment can be configured by adding the WorkerJavaScriptBackend.

@cloudflare/shell is deprecated, and so is Think's createExecuteTool. These will no longer be developed nor supported from today onwards.

Migrate your workspace data

This is a breaking change. @cloudflare/computer stores files in different tables from @cloudflare/shell, and there is no automatic data migration between workspace formats. To keep an existing workspace, copy its files with the script in Migrating from @cloudflare/shell to @cloudflare/computer ↗︎. Otherwise your agent will start with an empty workspace, though the original data will still be present in the existing tables.

For more information, refer to Think tools.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Wrangler and cf now upload source maps by default
item.description:
From Wrangler 4.150.0, wrangler deploy, wrangler versions upload, and wrangler preview generate and upload source maps by default. You no longer need to set upload_source_maps to get stack traces with your original file names and line numbers.

cf deploy also uploads source maps by default. With the Cloudflare Vite plugin 1.64.0 or later, Worker builds generate source maps by default, and cf deploy uploads every source map in the build output.

Remapped stack traces show up in Workers Logs, real-time logs, Tail Workers, and Workers Issues. Source maps are applied after your Worker runs, so they don't affect CPU time, bundle size, or cold starts.

If your Worker uses a custom build, Wrangler uploads any external source maps it finds. Maps it can't resolve, such as inline data: source maps, are skipped instead of failing the upload. Set upload_source_maps to true if you'd prefer the upload to fail.

To opt out with Wrangler, set upload_source_maps to false:

To opt out with cf or the Cloudflare Vite plugin, set build.sourcemap to false for your Worker's Vite environment. Refer to Disable source maps.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Test Cron Triggers with Local Explorer
item.description:
Local Explorer can now send one-off Cron Trigger invocations to a Worker's scheduled() handler during local development. This removes the need to construct request URLs when testing handler behavior.

Start your local development server with cf dev, wrangler dev, or the Cloudflare Vite plugin. Open /cdn-cgi/local/explorer on the server URL and select Cron Triggers.

The browser interface supports the following tasks:

  • Invoke configured cron expressions
  • Build ad hoc expressions
  • Set reusable scheduled times
  • Inspect outcomes and noRetry() status

Ad hoc triggers and scheduled time presets stay in your browser. They do not change cloudflare.config.ts, your Wrangler configuration, or deployed Cron Triggers. Local development does not run cron schedules automatically.

Full logs and traces are available in the development session that owns the Worker when that session has Observability turned on.

The following example uses port 8787. Replace it with your development server port, such as 5173 for Vite.

The Local Explorer API exposes the same operation for tools and AI agents. The request targets an exact Worker name and accepts a cron expression and optional scheduled time:

For more details, refer to Test Cron Triggers with Local Explorer.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Search Cloudflare documentation with the Cloudflare CLI
item.description:
Cloudflare CLI 1.0.0-beta.16 includes cf docs search, so you and your coding agent can find Cloudflare documentation without leaving the terminal. Search for guides, tutorials, and examples across Cloudflare products.

To install or update to the latest release:

npm install --global cf@latest
yarn global add cf@latest
pnpm add --global cf@latest
bun add --global cf@latest

Describe what you want to do, or ask a question:

The command searches live Cloudflare documentation and returns up to five ranked JSON results. Each result includes a title, description, and documentation URL. An Internet connection is required.

Agents can parse the results and fetch a complete page as Markdown. For example, use jq to select the first result, then request its URL with the Accept: text/markdown header:

This release also standardizes generated command names to kebab-case. For example, cf accounts billing getCredits becomes cf accounts billing get-credits. For the full list of breaking command and flag changes, refer to the Cloudflare CLI release notes ↗︎.

For more information, refer to Find Cloudflare documentation with a coding agent.

item.title: Cloudflare One, Workers, Gateway - Gateway and Workers integration is now in public beta
item.description:
Cloudflare Gateway now integrates with Cloudflare Workers in public beta on all Zero Trust plans. You can use the Forward action in Gateway HTTP policies to run your own code on matching, permitted traffic without managing a separate proxy.

The Forward action lets you transform HTTP requests and responses, return a coaching page, or run background tasks such as Slack notifications and R2 captures. Your Worker receives the request and Gateway context, including connection metadata, user identity, and device posture when available.

Gateway handles the proxy connection, TLS decryption, and upstream routing. It evaluates HTTP request policies before Forward policies and inspects the final response before returning it to the user.

Gateway inspects the original request body before delivering it to your Worker. A body-inspection Block decision can interrupt the Worker.

To get started, deploy a Worker and configure a Forward policy, or adapt one of the Worker templates.

item.title: Workers - Workers Builds now uses newer versions of Node.js, Python, Go, Bun, and more
item.description:
Your builds now run on newer versions of Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, Bun, Yarn, and Python package managers by default, so you get the latest fixes and features without changing your build configuration.

item.title: Agents, Workers - Cloudflare API MCP server sends Workers Issues as MCP Events
item.description:
Workers Issues provides built-in error monitoring for Cloudflare Workers. It detects production failures and groups related failures into issues without an SDK or application wrapper.

The Cloudflare API MCP server now sends these issues as MCP Events ↗︎, the first event it exposes. MCP clients discover cloudflare.alert.workers_observability_real_time_issue with events/list and subscribe with events/subscribe, scoped to an account or a single Worker. When Issues detects a new or recurring issue, the server posts a signed event to the client's webhook, so an agent can start investigating without polling.

To use it, enable Issues on your Worker and connect https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp with the Notifications Write and Workers Observability Write permissions to a client that supports MCP Events webhooks.

item.title: Agents, Workers - Run OpenCode 2.0 on Cloudflare with the Agents SDK
item.description:
The Agents SDK now supports OpenCode 2.0 ↗︎ through the experimental OpenCodeHarness. Run OpenCode inside a plain Durable Object, with sessions stored in SQLite and Lifecycle jobs that wake interrupted work after eviction.

The agents/models/opencode provider connects OpenCode to Workers AI through the AI binding. OpenCode plugins extend the harness with custom tools, remote MCP servers, and skills. Refer to OpenCode's Cloudflare SDK documentation ↗︎ for the embedded host API.

Install Agents SDK 0.28.0 or later with the OpenCode packages:

npm i agents@latest @opencode/sdk@2 @opencode/plugin@2
yarn add agents@latest @opencode/sdk@2 @opencode/plugin@2
pnpm add agents@latest @opencode/sdk@2 @opencode/plugin@2
bun add agents@latest @opencode/sdk@2 @opencode/plugin@2

Create a harness and install a Lifecycle on your Durable Object:

The OpenCode harness guide includes the workerTools plugin, Wrangler configuration, and session APIs. The working example ↗︎ adds a browser UI, WebSocket streaming, and Workspace tools from @cloudflare/computer for files and code execution.

item.title: Workers - Workers Builds now posts preview URLs in seconds
item.description:
Workers Builds now consistently posts preview URLs to GitHub pull requests and GitLab merge requests within a few seconds of a build completing, so you can start testing and reviewing your changes sooner. Previously, posting preview URLs could often take minutes.

For details, refer to Workers Builds GitHub integration and Workers Builds GitLab integration.

item.title: Workers - More time for requests to finish during Workers runtime updates
item.description:
Pending requests and connections to Workers now have a grace period of up to 20 minutes during Workers runtime updates. Previously, the grace period was up to 30 seconds.

This gives long-running HTTP requests, streamed AI responses, and live WebSocket sessions more time to continue before an update interrupts them.

New incoming HTTP requests go to the updated version of the Workers runtime once it is ready. Processes running the previous version stop accepting these requests and drain existing work. The grace period applies to each process running the previous version. When it ends, unfinished requests and open connections on that process are terminated.

You should design your application to reconnect WebSockets, safely retry interrupted requests, and recover saved state after a restart. WebSockets can disconnect before the grace period ends, including connections using the WebSocket Hibernation API.

For more information, refer to Workers runtime updates.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Create Workflow instance batches by count or list
item.description:
createBatch() now accepts an options object that creates up to 100 Workflow instances in one call. The result lists the created instances and explains why any others were not created. To use this form in local development and get its types from wrangler types, use Wrangler 4.148.0 or later.

To create instances that share the same options, pass count. Each instance receives a generated ID:

To give each instance its own ID or options, pass instances:

created contains the created instances. errors contains each entry that was not created, identified by its position in the input. IDs that already exist and IDs repeated within the batch are reported as errors instead of being skipped silently.

Passing an array to createBatch() is deprecated. Existing code that uses the array form continues to work.

For more information, refer to createBatch.

item.title: Agents, Workers - Run the Pi Durable harness on Cloudflare with the Agents SDK
item.description:
The Agents SDK now provides first-class support for building agents using the Pi harness. You can build long-running agents using the combination of Pi 1.0 ↗︎, Pi Durable ↗︎, and the new PiHarness class that the Cloudflare Agents SDK provides, ensuring your agent's work is durably persisted, even if interrupted mid-turn.

Built with Earendil ↗︎, this integration is our first step toward first-class support for third-party agent harnesses on Cloudflare.

Beta

PiHarness is in beta. Pi Durable ↗︎ is a new, experimental package, and the PiHarness API will likely change as Pi Durable matures.

PiHarness is a new "Lifecycle capability" provided by the Cloudflare Agents SDK. Pi Durable provides the agent harness and the Lifecycle is responsible for keeping the agent running in the Durable Object. The Lifecycle is a core concept in the Agents SDK ensuring that long-running work can run in a Durable Object, surviving restarts, crashes, and network issues. We will share more on Lifecycle capabilities in the near future.

Install

npm i agents@latest @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai
yarn add agents@latest @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai
pnpm add agents@latest @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai
bun add agents@latest @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai

Both Pi packages are optional peer dependencies of agents, so you only install them if you use the harness.

Use it in an Agent

Creating a Pi agent requires configuring the Pi Harness with a model, skills, and tools, then registering the PiHarness with the Agent class.

The agents/models/pi-ai entry point supports AI Gateway and Workers AI models, so you can get started with Cloudflare models right away or use your existing Pi AI provider.

Add tools with extensions

Both tools and system prompt sections are provided to the Pi Harness via extensions.

For more information on creating and configuring extensions, refer to Extensions.

Learn more

  • Pi harness documentation
  • Pi harness extensions
  • pi-ai model provider
  • Pi harness example ↗︎, with WebSockets, a browser UI, and a @cloudflare/computer Workspace for the model's tools
  • Lifecycle ↗︎
  • Pi Durable announcement ↗︎ from Earendil

item.title: Agents, Workers - The best way to do MCP auth just got better: Workers OAuth Provider goes v1, with a new split API and full support for MCP 2026-07-28
item.description:
@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider ↗︎ is now v1, with a new split API. One Worker acts as the authorization server: it signs users in and issues tokens. Your MCP server acts as the resource server, and can run in another Worker. It validates each token with the authorization server over a Service Binding, without crossing the public Internet.

  • It supports the MCP 2026-07-28 authorization specification ↗︎, including Client ID Metadata Documents ↗︎ and issuer identification ↗︎. It still works with older clients, including those using Dynamic Client Registration ↗︎.
  • insufficientScope() gives you step-up authorization ↗︎ in one line.
  • The authorization server and the resource server can run in different Workers ↗︎ with different WAF and rate limiting rules.
  • One authorization server can issue tokens for many MCP servers ↗︎.
  • A migration skill ↗︎ ships in the npm package so a coding agent can perform the upgrade.

The split API

In the example, env.AUTH_SERVER.validateToken is that Service Binding call. The calendar Worker needs no KV namespace of its own.

OAuthResourceServer publishes the RFC 9728 ↗︎ protected resource metadata that MCP clients use to find your authorization server. It answers requests without a token with a 401 challenge that points to that metadata. It also rejects tokens issued for any other resource.

You can still use OAuthProvider as both the authorization server and the MCP server. For most 0.x deployments, the only required change is to add resourceMetadata: { resource }.

Other updates and helpers

  • Consent page ↗︎ and upstream sign-in ↗︎ helpers implement the MCP confused deputy protections.
  • Sliding refresh token expiry ↗︎ with refreshTokenIdleTTL.
  • Resumable KV cleanup ↗︎ with purgeExpiredData().
  • An internal reason ↗︎ on every error passed to onError.

Upgrade with the migration skill

npm i @cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider@latest
yarn add @cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider@latest
pnpm add @cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider@latest
bun add @cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider@latest

Point your coding agent at node_modules/@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider/skills/migrate-to-1.x/SKILL.md, or follow the migration guide ↗︎.

For both Workers in full, refer to the split Workers example ↗︎.

item.title: Artifacts, Workers - Artifacts is now in open beta
item.description:
Artifacts, Cloudflare's versioned file system that speaks Git, is now in open beta. Artifacts is built for scale, so you can create a repository per project, user, session, or task.

With Artifacts, you can:

  • Programmatically manage repositories — Use an Artifacts binding from a Worker to create or fork repos, inspect files and commits, read files by path, and issue repo-scoped Git tokens.

Artifacts is available for customers on the Workers Paid plan. Cloudflare will begin billing for Artifacts on October 14, 2026.

Build the next GitHub on Cloudflare

Apply today ↗︎ — submissions are open until October 14, 2026.

The first-place team will receive $25,000 in Cloudflare credits. The top three teams will be flown to San Francisco to present what they built at Cloudflare Connect.

item.title: Workers - Web Crypto adds ML-KEM and ML-DSA support
item.description:
The Workers Web Crypto API now supports ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87. ML-KEM establishes shared secrets, while ML-DSA signs and verifies data.

The opt-in API also adds key encapsulation and decapsulation methods, getPublicKey(), SubtleCrypto.supports(), and JSON Web Keys (JWKs) with the AKP key type.

Turn on the webcrypto_modern_algorithms compatibility flag to use these features:

This example uses ML-KEM-768 to establish the same shared secret on both sides:

Workers implements a subset of the evolving Modern Algorithms in the Web Cryptography API ↗︎ draft. ML-KEM-512 and the draft's other algorithms are not supported. The API may change as the draft evolves.

For current algorithm and operation support, refer to Web Crypto supported algorithms.

item.title: Workers - Workers Cache — mark cached responses stale with invalidate()
item.description:
Workers Cache now supports invalidate(), the soft counterpart of purge(). purge() deletes matching cached responses, so the next request is a cache miss. invalidate() keeps them but marks them stale, so the cache revalidates them with your Worker instead.

To revalidate a response, the cache sends your Worker a conditional request built from the validators stored with it — for example, If-None-Match carrying the cached ETag. If your Worker answers 304 Not Modified, the cache keeps the stored body. If your Worker answers with a full 200 response, that response replaces the cached one.

invalidate() accepts the same options as purge(): tags, pathPrefixes, or purgeEverything. It follows the same per-entrypoint scoping and resolves to the same result object. Call it as ctx.cache.invalidate(), or import cache from cloudflare:workers and call cache.invalidate().

Use invalidate() when one call covers many cached responses but only some of them changed. Your Worker needs to emit ETag or Last-Modified and answer matching conditional requests with 304. Each unchanged response then costs a validator check instead of a full regeneration:

For more information, refer to Invalidate cached responses.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Cloudflare CLI is now in beta
item.description:
The Cloudflare CLI, cf, is now in beta. cf is one command-line interface for the public Cloudflare API and for Workers projects. Use it to manage zones, DNS, storage, and security settings, and to create, develop, and deploy Workers, without switching between tools.

Install cf globally, then sign in:

npm install --global cf
yarn global add cf
pnpm add --global cf
bun add --global cf

With cf, you can:

  • Manage resources across Cloudflare. More than 2,900 commands cover the public Cloudflare API, and most print their results as JSON.
  • Create and deploy Workers. cf init creates a project that uses cloudflare.config.ts, a typed configuration file. cf dev, cf build, and cf deploy develop, build, and deploy it.
  • Move from Wrangler. cf migrate converts a Wrangler configuration file to cloudflare.config.ts. You can also run cf resource commands in an existing Wrangler project without migrating it.
  • Work with coding agents. cf cli search finds the command for a task from a plain-language description, so an agent can find and run commands without prior knowledge of cf.

cf is in beta. Commands, configuration, and Build Output can change before the stable release.

To get started, refer to Install and sign in. To move an existing project, refer to Migrate a Wrangler project.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Call Workflows declared in `exports` through `ctx.exports`
item.description:
A Worker can now call the Workflows it declares in the exports field of its Wrangler configuration through ctx.exports. You no longer need a workflows binding to call a Workflow from the Worker that defines it.

Each Workflow is keyed by class name, and has the same API as a Workflow binding:

A workflows binding and a workflow export with the same name share their instances. You can move a Workflow from a binding to an export without losing its instances.

wrangler dev, the Cloudflare Vite plugin, and the Workers Vitest integration run Workflows on ctx.exports locally. Local development requires Wrangler 4.142.0, @cloudflare/vite-plugin 1.61.0, or @cloudflare/vitest-plugin 1.3.0 or above.

In Vitest, introspectWorkflow() and introspectWorkflowInstance() still need a Workflow binding. To introspect a Workflow declared in exports, add a test-only binding to it.

For more information, refer to Call a Workflow through ctx.exports.

item.title: Workers - Workers tracing — new getActiveSpan(), recordException(), startSpan(), and setAttributes() APIs
item.description:
Custom spans in Workers now support more of the OpenTelemetry span API, so you can instrument more of your code and record errors directly on your spans.

  • tracing.startSpan(name) creates a span without making it the active span, and returns it. Other spans do not nest under it. Call span.end() when the operation is complete.
  • tracing.getActiveSpan() returns the currently active span. Use it to annotate the current span from helper functions and libraries without passing the span object through your code. Outside any custom span, it returns the invocation's root span.
  • span.recordException(exception) records an exception event on a span. It accepts an Error, a string, or an object with a code, name, or message.
  • span.setAttributes(attributes) sets multiple attributes at once. setAttribute() and setAttributes() now return the span, so you can chain calls.

For more details, refer to the custom spans documentation.

item.title: Workers - See every release and gradual deployment on Workers Metrics charts
item.description:
Workers Metrics charts now show every release in the selected time range, including the full progression of gradual deployments. This makes it easier to correlate changes in memory, CPU time, errors, or latency with the code that was serving traffic.

A gradual deployment appears as a single rollout across the chart, with shading that increases as more traffic moves to the new version. Hover over a rollout to see the previous and new versions, the rollout duration, and the traffic percentage configured at each step.

Use these annotations to:

  • Find when a regression started — See which traffic percentage was configured when errors, latency, CPU time, or wall time changed.
  • Compare rollout stages — Check whether a metric changed as more traffic moved to the new version.
  • Confirm rollbacks — Rollbacks appear as separate release events, so you can check whether metrics recovered after a rollback.

Direct deployments that send 100% of traffic to a single version still appear as individual markers. Nearby direct deployments are grouped to reduce visual clutter. Versions that are only uploaded, or only configured at 0%, do not appear on metrics charts.

To view release annotations, open the Metrics tab for your Worker ↗︎.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Declare Workflows in the `exports` configuration
item.description:
You can now declare the Workflows a Worker defines in the exports field of your Wrangler configuration file. Previously, a Worker could only define a Workflow through a workflows binding, even when the Worker never called the Workflow itself.

Key each entry by the name of the class that extends WorkflowEntrypoint:

A workflow export accepts the same settings as a workflows binding: limits, schedules, and default_retention. When you run wrangler deploy, Wrangler creates or updates the Workflow with these settings.

You can declare a Workflow as both a binding and an export. Both declarations must use the same class, and cannot set the same setting to different values.

A workflows binding to a Workflow in another Worker cannot use the same name as a Workflow export in this Worker. Workflow names are unique per account.

Workflow exports require Wrangler 4.139.0 or above.

For more information, refer to Declare Workflows in exports.

item.title: Workers - Workers Builds now supports Cursor Origin
item.description:
Workers Builds now supports repositories hosted in Cursor Origin. Connect a Cursor Origin repository to automatically build and deploy production changes, preview non-production branches, and see build status in pull requests.

Pushes to your production branch automatically build and deploy your Worker. When you enable non-production branch builds, each branch receives a version-specific preview URL and a stable preview URL that follows the latest build.

Cloudflare posts build status and preview links to the Cursor Origin pull request and creates a check run for each triggered build.

To get started, install the Cloudflare app in Cursor ↗︎, choose the Cursor Origin repositories Cloudflare can access, and follow the prompts to configure your Worker build. For details, refer to the Cursor Origin integration.

item.title: Workers - Test every pull request in an isolated environment with Worker Previews
item.description:
You can now test every change you make in an isolated, production-like environment with Worker Previews ↗︎. Each Preview runs under the same Worker with its own code, configuration, URL, and observability, isolated from production and every other Preview.

Configure each Preview

Define the variables, bindings, and settings that new Previews start with in the previews block of your Wrangler configuration file. Set secrets with Wrangler commands. You can override one Preview without changing production or other Previews.

For Durable Objects and Containers, Cloudflare automatically provisions separate namespaces, storage, apps, and instances for every Preview. State changes, sessions, memory, migrations, and concurrent tests remain scoped to that Preview. To isolate KV, D1, R2, or another account-level resource, bind the Preview to a separate resource.

Deploy and share every change

Use Wrangler 4.135.0 or later to deploy a Preview:

Or connect your repository to Workers Builds to create Previews automatically and post their URLs to pull requests.

Each Preview gets a stable URL that updates with every push, so reviewers always see the latest changes. Each deployment also gets an immutable URL, so you can compare or return to an exact version.

After you create a Preview, use the environment breadcrumb next to your Worker's name to switch between Production and every Preview:

Inspect and revise before production

Each Preview has its own logs, errors, metrics, and traces. Send traffic to its URL, inspect what happened, push a fix, and verify the next deployment before production.

Use production-like hostnames

Serve Preview URLs on workers.dev, a custom domain, or both. Custom domains let authentication providers, cookies, cross-origin resource sharing (CORS), and OAuth redirects work as they will in production. You can also protect Preview URLs with Cloudflare Access.

Configure a domain for Preview traffic from the Worker's Domains tab:

For setup instructions and current limitations, refer to the Worker Previews documentation.

item.title: Workers - Give teammates access to specific Workers directly from the dashboard
item.description:
You can now grant teammates scoped access to specific Workers directly from the Workers dashboard.

Go to your Worker and click Invite.

Enter the teammate's email address, choose the appropriate access level, and click Invite.

You can grant a user one of the following access levels:

  • Metadata Read-Only: View settings, metrics, logs, and traces without access to Worker code or the ability to make changes.
  • Content Read-Only: Read Worker code, settings, and observability data without the ability to modify or deploy changes.
  • Editor: Update and deploy a Worker without the ability to delete it.
  • Admin: Everything included with Editor, plus the ability to delete the Worker.

If the teammate is already an account member, they will receive access to the Worker immediately. If they are not an account member, Cloudflare will send them an invitation to join the account, and they will receive access to the Worker after accepting the invitation.

Only account members with the Super Administrator role can invite users from a Worker's dashboard.

For details about available roles and scopes, refer to the Workers roles and permissions documentation.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Delete Workflow instances individually or in batches
item.description:
You can now delete one or up to 100 Workflow instances and their stored state via the Workflows API or Wrangler 4.125.0 and later. Deleting an instance frees its stored state and stops its current execution. Storage billing is based on the average daily peak.

Delete one instance by calling delete() on its handle:

If a Workflow deletes its own instance, execution stops during await instance.delete(). Code after the call does not run.

Delete multiple instances by calling deleteBatch() on the Workflow binding:

The batch result contains { id } entries for successful deletions and per-instance errors. IDs that do not exist are returned as errors. Duplicate IDs count toward the limit and are deleted once, with the result repeated for each input position.

Wrangler accepts positional instance IDs, a file containing a top-level JSON array of strings, or both, up to 100 IDs total. Use latest to delete the most recently created instance. Use --local against a local wrangler dev session:

For more information, refer to Delete Workflow instances, delete, and deleteBatch.

item.title: Workers, Durable Objects - Workers traces now automatically include JavaScript RPC session spans
item.description:
Workers traces can now follow JavaScript RPC calls across Worker boundaries and into Durable Objects. Previously, a trace stopped at the caller's RPC boundary. The dashboard now shows the caller-side session and method calls alongside the callee invocation, nested calls, and callbacks into another Worker.

A session span covers the lifetime of a caller-side session and groups calls that reuse it. Individual call spans show each method invocation. Execution colors distinguish the Workers or Durable Object entrypoints involved, while arrows mark outgoing and incoming calls. Together, these details show where time was spent, which calls reused a session, and how returned stubs and callbacks fit into the request.

Enable tracing with one setting in your Wrangler configuration file:

Cloudflare records these spans automatically. You do not need to change your application code or add an observability SDK.

For supported spans and attributes, refer to Spans and attributes.

item.title: Workers, Hyperdrive - Hyperdrive support for Python Workers
item.description:
Python Workers can now connect to PostgreSQL and MySQL through Hyperdrive.

For setup, code examples, and limitations, refer to Use Hyperdrive from Python Workers.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Stream Workflow instance events in your Worker or via the API with .subscribe()
item.description:
You can now stream Workflow instance events via WorkflowInstance.subscribe() and the GET /subscribe API endpoint. Workers and HTTP clients can react to workflow and step events, including attempts, sleeps, waits, and rollbacks, without polling for instance status.

A subscription first streams the entire event history of the Workflow instance. After streaming past events, the subscription waits for new events as the instance runs. You can use filter to receive only specific event types or cursor to start a subscription at a specific event.

Use .subscribe() to update Workflow status in user-facing dashboards, send notifications when steps complete, or trigger follow-up work for specific events.

For event types, available fields, and subscription options, refer to Subscribe to events.

item.title: Workers - Grant teammates and agents access to specific Workers
item.description:
You can now grant access to specific Workers and choose from four roles to control the level of access you give teammates, agents, and CI/CD workflows.

Choose from four roles to control the level of access:

  • Metadata Read-Only: View settings, metrics, logs, and traces without access to Worker code or the ability to make changes.
  • Content Read-Only: Read Worker code, settings, and observability data without the ability to modify or deploy changes.
  • Editor: Update and deploy a Worker without the ability to delete it.
  • Admin: Everything in Editor, plus the ability to delete the Worker.

Worker-level access controls are available today for all customers. You can configure them in the Cloudflare dashboard, through the API, or with Terraform.

Roles designed for how teams build

Give Metadata Read-Only to a debugging agent so it can inspect settings and observability data without seeing Worker code. Give Content Read-Only to a code review agent so it can read code without changing it. Give Editor to a CI/CD workflow so it can deploy without deleting the Worker or accessing other Workers. Admin gives a teammate or agent full control over the Worker, including the ability to delete it.

Apply these roles across all Developer Platform products, across all Workers, or to an individual Worker.

Durable Objects

You can use granular permissions to control access to Durable Objects. Durable Objects do not have their own roles or scopes. Instead, they inherit the permissions assigned to the Worker that implements them.

Learn more about granular permissions in the Durable Objects documentation.

Grant access to members and User Groups

In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to Manage Account > Members and select a member. Create a permission policy, set the scope to Individual Workers, select the Workers they need, and choose a role to grant the right level of access.

If several people on the same team or project need the same access, assign the permission policy to a User Group instead of each member individually. Everyone added to the group automatically inherits the policy.

Create a scoped API token

For an agent or CI/CD workflow, go to Manage Account > Account API Tokens and create an account-owned API token. Set the scope to Specified Workers, select the Workers the token can access, and choose a role to grant the right level of access.

For more information, refer to the Workers roles and permissions documentation.

item.title: Workers - Miniflare v5 prepares local development for the cf CLI
item.description:
Miniflare v5 prepares Cloudflare local development tooling for the upcoming cf CLI.

Miniflare powers local Workers development behind wrangler dev, the Cloudflare Vite plugin, and @cloudflare/vitest-plugin. Most projects should use those tools instead of depending on Miniflare directly, and Miniflare v5 will not require any action.

The most significant change is a new configuration shape which aligns Miniflare with cloudflare.config.ts, the programmatic Cloudflare configuration format now available for testing.

Other breaking changes include:

  • Removed deprecated APIs and options, such as legacy alpha D1 bindings.
  • Removed now-unused, internal APIs like wrappedBindings
  • Removed Miniflare's built-in module discovery; higher-level tools like Wrangler and the Vite plugin should be providing the module graph.
  • Moved local-only /cdn-cgi routes under /cdn-cgi/local.
  • Replaced per-resource persistence options with shared persistence root options.

For a more comprehensive list, refer to Miniflare's changelog ↗︎

This work sets up a cleaner foundation for the next generation of local development tooling, including the new cf CLI.

item.title: Workers - Python 3.14 for Python Workers
item.description:
Python workers now use Python 3.14 by default.

This change applies to all new Python workers using compatibility date 2026-09-08 or later.

Internally, this change updates the Pyodide runtime to 314.0.6.

item.title: Email Service, Workers - Manage Email Routing rules with Wrangler
item.description:
You can now manage Email Routing rules that route emails to Workers from your Wrangler configuration. Add literal addresses or a catch-all address to the top-level addresses field:

When you run wrangler deploy, Wrangler creates rules for new addresses, updates existing rules managed by the Worker, and removes managed rules that are no longer in the configuration. Wrangler shows the planned changes and asks for confirmation before applying potentially destructive changes.

Email Routing rules created by Wrangler also appear in the dashboard but with an icon that identifies them.

Refer to Configure rules with Wrangler for more information.

item.title: Cloudflare Fundamentals, Workers - Enterprise customers can self-serve CDN upload limits up to 5 GB
item.description:
Enterprise customers can now configure a zone's CDN Maximum Upload Size up to 5 GB directly from the Network page in the Cloudflare dashboard. This removes the need to contact your account team or Cloudflare Support when applications need to accept request bodies larger than 500 MB and no greater than 5 GB.

The default maximum upload size remains 500 MB. Upload limits above 5 GB still require additional configuration through your account team or Cloudflare Support.

Very large uploads may reach connection or read timeouts before reaching the configured size limit. Make sure clients and origins allow enough time to complete the transfer when increasing this setting.

Refer to Cache upload limits and Workers request body size limits for details.

item.title: Workers - Deploy larger Workers — up to 64 MiB for both free and paid plans
item.description:
You can now deploy Workers with larger dependencies, heavier frameworks, and more code without hitting size limits.

When you deploy a Worker, Wrangler bundles your code and compresses it before uploading. Previously, Cloudflare checked that compressed size and rejected deploys over 3 MB (Free) or 10 MB (Paid). That limit has been removed. Cloudflare now only checks the uncompressed size of your bundle, which is 64 MiB across all plans.

To check your Worker's bundle size before deploying:

The Total Upload value is your uncompressed bundle size. This is what counts against the 64 MiB limit. The gzip value is shown for reference but is no longer a limit.

For more information, refer to the Worker size limits documentation.

item.title: Workers - Python Workers now support WSGI web frameworks like Django and Flask
item.description:
Python web frameworks following the Web Server Gateway Interface (WSGI) ↗︎ or Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface (ASGI) ↗︎ specification can now be used in Python Workers.

Using web frameworks with Python Workers
